extraction_notes.note: Definition or algorithm: the pathwise construction of the Walsh process (excursions sent to edge k with probability w_k) is a recipe, but it serves to define the process W, so it is one definition node.

Definition or external theorem: the sentence applies Dynkin's formula for the generator at v, but what it introduces and what later nodes use is the exit time H^w_{v,epsilon}. Typed as that definition.

Remark or claim: each paragraph argues and concludes in one go (K_s is a stopping time; L^s is the local time of W^s; v is not a trap) with no separately stated result. RP11 is relied on later, in DP52.

The second proof of Theorem 3.2 is taken from 'With lemma 3.3 ...'. The earlier sentence that specializes (1.30) to the elastic process sits before Lemma 3.4 and is left outside the proof, so the lemma does not have to be nested in it.

In prose, the definitions of the killed processes and the claims that they are Brownian motions are interleaved. W^g is defined in the same sentence that asserts it is a Brownian motion, so it is a single definition node.

The defined-term check flags every 'Brownian motion'. Edges from DP7 go only to uses meaning a Brownian motion on the star graph; the many uses meaning standard or reflected Brownian motion on the line get none.

Left out: the introduction's survey and outline, the heuristic paragraph explaining why the vertex is 'sticky', convention sentences ('for the remainder of this section we choose a=c=0, w_k=b_k'), and the cited limits of g_{beta,gamma} as beta or gamma tend to 0.
The finishing step warns that the prose node starts mid-sentence. It starts right after a \vspace command at a real sentence start, so the warning is a false alarm.

\label{rem2.4}
The matrix $\ensuremath S^w=\bigl(\ensuremath S^w_{km},\,k,m = 1,\dotsc,n\bigr)$ is the \emph{scattering
matrix} as defined in quantum mechanics. We briefly recall its construction in the
present context, for more details the interested reader is referred
to~\cite{KoSc99}. $\ensuremath S^w$ is obtained from the boundary conditions at the vertex $v$
in the following way. Consider a function $f$ on $\mathcal{G}$ which is continuously
differentiable in $\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ=\mathcal{G}\setminus\{v\}$, and such that for all $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$ the limits
\begin{align*}
    F_k  &= f(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\ensuremath^\circ} f(\xi)\\
    F'_k &= f'(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\ensuremath^\circ} f'(\xi)
\end{align*}
exist. Define two column vectors $F$, $F'\in\mathbb{C}^n$, having the components $F_k$ and
$F'_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, respectively. Furthermore, consider boundary conditions of the following
form
\begin{equation}    \label{bc}
    A F + B F' =0,
\end{equation}
where $A$ and $B$ are complex $n\times n$ matrices. The \emph{on-shell scattering
matrix at energy $E>0$} is defined as
\begin{equation}    \label{SE}
    S_{A,B}(E) = - (A+i\sqrt{E}B)^{-1}(A-i\sqrt{E}B),
\end{equation}
which exists and is unitary, provided the $n\times 2n$ matrix $(A,B)$ has
maximal rank (i.e., rank $n$) and $AB^\dagger$ is hermitian. These requirements for $A$
and $B$ guarantee that the corresponding Laplace operator is self-adjoint
on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ (with Lebesgue measure). Observe that under these conditions the
boundary conditions~\eqref{bc} are equivalent to any boundary conditions of the form
$CAF+CBF'=0$ where $C$ is invertible. Also $S_{CA, CB}(E) = S_{A,B}(E)$ holds true.
For the Walsh process at hand, concrete choices for $A$ and $B$ are given by
\begin{equation*}
    A^w=\begin{pmatrix}
            0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\
            1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\
            0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\
            0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\
            \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
            0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1
        \end{pmatrix},\ 
    B^w=\begin{pmatrix}
            b_1&b_2&b_3&\ldots&b_{n-1}&b_n\\
            0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\
            0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\
            \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
            0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\
            0&0&0&\ldots&0&0
        \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
Then~\eqref{bc} is the condition that $f$ is actually continuous at the vertex $v$,
i.e., $f(v_k)=f(v_m)$, $k$, $m=1,\dotsc,n$, and that~\eqref{eq2.2} is valid (with
$w_k=b_k$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$). Obviously, $(A^w, B^w)$ has maximal rank. However, $A^w
(B^w)^\dagger$ is hermitian if and only if all $b_k$ are equal (i.e., $b_k = 1/n$,
$\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$). Nevertheless, \eqref{SE} exists also in the non-hermitian case, and $S_{A^w,
B^w}(E)=S^w$ holds for all $E>0$ due to the relations $A^w S^w = - A^w$, and $B^w
S^w = B^w$. In addition, the following relations are valid:
\begin{align}
         \ensuremath S^w &= \bigl(\ensuremath S^w\bigr)^{-1}, \label{eq2.5}\\
    \det \ensuremath S^w &= (-1)^{n+1}.           \label{eq2.6}
\end{align}
Furthermore, $S^w$ is a contraction, and the associated Laplace operator is
m-dissipative on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ since trivially $\text{Im}(AB^\dagger)=0$, cf.\ Theorem~2.5
in~\cite{KoPo09c}. When all $b_k$ are equal, such that $A^w(B^w)^\dag=0$, then $S^w$ is
an involutive, orthogonal matrix of the form
\begin{equation}	\label{eq2.6a}
	S^w = - \1 + 2P_n.
\end{equation}
$P_n$ is the matrix whose entries are equal to $1/n$.
$P_n$ is a real orthogonal projection, that is $P_n = P_n^\dag = P_n^t = P_n^2$.
It is also of rank $1$, that is $\dim \text{Ran} P_n = 1$.
The relation~\eqref{eq2.4b} giving the resolvent in terms of the
scattering matrix is actually valid in the more general context of arbitrary metric
graphs and boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc}, see~\cite{KoSc06, KoPo09c}.

We may consider the Walsh process $W$ as being pathwise constructed from a standard
Brownian motion $B$ on the real line as in the previous section, and we shall use
the notations and conventions from there. Then it is clear that under $P_v$ and
under $\ensuremath{\hat P}_v$, $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ has the same law as the hitting time of the point
$\epsilon$ in $\mathbb{R}_+$ by the reflecting Brownian motion $|B|$ under $Q_0$, that is, as
$H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}}$ of the Brownian motion $B$ itself under $Q_0$. Let $K^w$ denote
the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^w$. For fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$ we get
\begin{equation*}
    \{K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\} = \{L^w(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})>s\}.
\end{equation*}
Hence
\begin{align*}
    P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)
        &= P_v\bigl(L^w(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})>s\bigr)\\
        &= Q_0\bigl(L^B(H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}})>s\bigr).
\end{align*}
In appendix~B of~\cite{BMMG0} is shown with the method
in~\cite[Section~6.4]{KaSh91} that under $Q_0$ the random variable
$L^B(H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}})$ is exponentially distributed with mean $\epsilon$. So we find
\begin{equation*}
    P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) = e^{-s/\epsilon}.
\end{equation*}
We integrate this relation against the exponential law with rate $\beta$ in the variable $s$,
and obtain
\begin{align*}
    \ensuremath{\hat P}_v\bigl(\zeta_{\beta,0}>\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)
        &= 1 - \beta\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta s}\,P_v\bigl(K^W_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)\,ds\\
        &= \frac{1}{1+\epsilon\beta}.
\end{align*}
We used the fact that due to the continuity of the paths of $W$ we have
$\zeta_{\beta,0}\ne \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$.

exactly when the underlying standard Brownian motion $B$ (cf.\ section~\ref{sect2})

Let $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, and $\gamma$ be defined as in~\eqref{eq4.4}, and note that due to the
condition~\eqref{eq1.1a} on $b_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, and $c$, we have $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$,
$\sum_k w_k =1$, as well as $\gamma>0$. Hence we can construct the associated sticky
Walsh process $\ensuremath W^s$ as above.

Let $A^s$ denote the generator of $\ensuremath W^s$ with domain $\mathcal{D}(A^s)$. Then we
have for $f\in\mathcal{D}(A^s)$, $A^s f(v) = 1/2 f''(v)$ (cf.\ theorem~\ref{thm_Feller}). On the
other hand, we can compute $A^s f(v)$ via Dynkin's formula as follows
\begin{align*}
    A^s f(v)
        &= \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \frac{E_v\Bigl(f\bigl(\ensuremath W^s(\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon})\bigr)\Bigr)-f(v)}
                                 {E_v\bigl(\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)}\\[1ex]
        &= \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \frac{\sum_k w_k f_k(\epsilon) - f(v)}{\epsilon^2 + \gamma\epsilon},
\end{align*}
where we used corollary~\ref{cor4.4}. Since the directional derivatives of $f$ at $v$
\begin{equation*}
    f'(v_k)=\lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k}    \frac{f(\xi)-f(v)}{d(\xi,v)},\qquad k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\},
\end{equation*}
exist (cf.\ lemma~\ref{lemC02}), we obviously get the boundary condition
\begin{equation}    \label{eq4.7}
    \frac{1}{2}\,f''(v) = \frac{1}{\gamma}\,\sum_{k=1}^n w_k f'(v_k)
\end{equation}
as a necessary condition. Finally, inserting of the values~\eqref{eq4.4} of the
parameters $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, and $\gamma$ into equation~\eqref{eq4.7} we complete the proof
of theorem~\ref{thm4.2}.

nodes.statement: When all w_m, m=1, dots, n, are equal to 1/n, the matrix S^s(lambda) takes the form S^s(lambda) = -\1 + frac2ensuremathsqrt2lambdaensuremathsqrt2lambda + gamma lambda\,P_n which reduces to~ when gamma=0. S^s(lambda) is unitary for all lambda<0. Also the S^s(lambda) for different lambda all commute. As a consequence S^s(lambda) has the interpretation of a quantum scattering matrix in the sense of. More precisely, S^s(lambda) stems from the Schr\"odinger operator -Delta^s, where Delta^s is a self-adjoint Laplace operator on L^2(G) with boundary conditions of the form~ with the choice A &= - frac12\,bigl(S^s(lambda_0)+\1bigr),\\ B &= - frac12sqrtmathstrut2lambda_0\,bigl(S^s(lambda_0)-\1bigr), for any lambda_0 for which sqrt2lambda_0+gammalambda_0ne 0. We emphasize that the Schr\"odinger operator -Delta^s and the generator A^s of the Walsh process are quite different: Not only do they act on different Banach spaces, but also the functions in the intersection of their domains satisfy different boundary conditions at the vertex v. As matter of fact, the integral kernel of the resolvent (-Delta^s+2lambda)^-1 of the Schr\"odinger operator -Delta^s is given by, see Lemma~4.2 in, frac12Bigl(r_lambda(xi,eta) +sum_k,m=1^n e_lambda,k(xi)\, ensuremath S^s_km(lambda)\,frac1ensuremathsqrt2lambda\,e_lambda,m(eta)Bigl), that is --- up to a factor 2 --- by the right hand side of~ without the last term. In more detail and with the definition~ S_A,Bbigl(E=-2lambdabigr) = S^s(lambda) holds for all lambda>0. As a function of k (k^2=E), S^s is meromorphic in the complex k--plane with a pole on the positive imaginary axis at k^b=2i/gamma. This corresponds to a negative eigenvalue E^b=-4/gamma^2 of -Delta^s. The corresponding (normalized) eigenfunction psi^b --- physically speaking a bound state --- is given as psi^b(xi) = frac12\,sqrtfracgamman\,e^-2 d(v,xi)/gamma, xiinG. So quantum mechanically the vertex v acts like an attractive potential. We view this as a quantum analogue of the stickiness of the vertex v. This analogy can be elaborated a bit further by inspecting the associated quantum mechanical time delay matrix (see, e.g., ) T(k) = frac12ik\,S(k)^-1fracpartialpartial k S(k) which in the present context gives T(k) = frac-2gammak(4+k^2gamma^2)\,P_n. So T(k) has zero as an (n-1)--fold eigenvalue plus the non-degenerate eigenvalue frac-2gammak(4+k^2gamma^2), which for gamma>0 is the signal for a strict quantum delay. Observe that for kto +infty, that is for large energies, the time delay experienced by the quantum particle tends to zero, while for kto 0, i.e., for low energies, the delay becomes arbitrarily large. From the physical point of view, both effects are clearly to be expected. For comparison and in contrast to the present stochastic context, in quantum mechanics gamma<0 is also allowed for a meaningful Schr\"odinger operator and an associated scattering matrix.

As in the previous cases it is readily seen that the definition~\eqref{eq5.5a} of
the parameters $\gamma$, $\beta$, $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, is consistent with the conditions used in
the above construction of $\ensuremath W^g$.

Let $A^g$ be the generator of $\ensuremath W^g$ with domain $\mathcal{D}(A^g)$. Since $\ensuremath W^g$ is a Brownian
motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}, it follows from
theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} that $\mathcal{D}(A^g)\subset \ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$, and that for all $f\in\mathcal{D}(A^g)$,
$A^g f(\xi) = 1/2\,f''(\xi)$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$. Let $h\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $\lambda>0$. Then $\ensuremath R^g_\lambda
h\in\mathcal{D}(A^g)$, and therefore we may compute with equation~\eqref{eq5.4} as follows
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v)
        &= \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)''(v)
            - \beta\,\rho(\lambda)\,2\lambda \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v)\\
        &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k)
            - \beta\,\rho(\lambda)\,\gamma\lambda \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v),
\end{align*}
where we used the fact that, since $\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h$ is in the domain of the generator $A^s$ of
$\ensuremath W^s$, it satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq4.7}. We rewrite this equation
in the following way:
\begin{equation}    \label{eq5.5}
\begin{split}
    \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v)
        = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k)
                &+\beta\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\rho(\lambda) \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v)\\
                &-\beta\,\rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda\bigr)\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\Bigr)(v).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Now we differentiate equation~\eqref{eq5.4} at $\xi\in l_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, let $\xi$ tend to
$v$ along any edge $l_k$, and sum the resulting equation against the weights $w_k$,
$\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$. Then we get the following formula
\begin{equation}    \label{eq5.6}
    \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k)
        = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k)
            + \beta\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v),
\end{equation}
where we used $\sum_k w_k=1$. On the other hand, for $\xi=v$, equation~\eqref{eq5.4}
gives
\begin{equation}    \label{eq5.7}
    \bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)(v) = \rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} +\gamma\lambda\bigr)\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v).
\end{equation}
A comparison of equations~\eqref{eq5.6}, \eqref{eq5.7} with \eqref{eq5.5} shows
that we have proved the following formula
\begin{equation}    \label{eq5.8}
    \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v)
        = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) - \beta \bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)(v).
\end{equation}
With the values~\eqref{eq5.5a} for $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, it is obvious that
$f=\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h$ satisfies equation~\eqref{eq1.1b}. Since $\ensuremath R^g_\lambda$ is surjective from
$\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ onto the domain of the generator $A^g$ of $\ensuremath W^g$, the proof of the theorem is finished.
